newsitem.title: FRANCE: France says immigrant review serves family, nation.
newsitem.headline: France says immigrant review serves family, nation.

text.p: France's new leftist government announced what it called humane criteria on Tuesday for deciding whether immigrants in legal limbo may stay in the country.
Interior Minister Jean-Pierre Chevenement said the national interest and the right to a family life would be key guidelines.

A case-by-case review of up to 40,000 possibly illegal immigrants would reflect France's traditional openness to foreign students and teachers and respect the European convention on human rights concerning families, he said.

"France must remain a country where students, teachers and researchers from around the world are welcome," Chevenement said in a speech to government prefects, who will be in charge of carrying out the controversial review.
Rightist deputies later booed and hooted who Chevenement sought to explain the review during parliamentary questioning.
"I find you very intolerant. You could lend an ear even if don't wish to be informed," Chevenement shouted back.
The centre-right, swept from power in a June 1 parliamentary election, had launched a crack-down on immigrants of uncertain status as well as those clearly lacking residence rights.
Chevenement said an immigration law enacted this year, far from clarifying the situation, had only confused things further, requiring a new reform to be put to parliament later this year.
In the meantime prefects, the central government's representatives in the provinces, would be asked to review all cases in which an immigrant's status was unclear, he said.
Those allowed to stay would include:
- spouses of French nationals, of foreigners residing legally in France, or of political refugees;
- children of foreigners residing legally in France;
- foreigners who are seriously ill;
- students pursuing advanced studies;
- individuals who would be in serious danger if they returned to their country of origin, and
- certain foreigners who have been in France for a long time or who are well integrated into French society.

Prime Minister Lionel Jospin said in his maiden policy address to parliament last week that he would seek legislation restoring the automatic right to French citizenship for anyone born on French soil. That right had been limited by the previous conservative government.

He said the case-by-case review of so-called "sans-papiers" -- people without residence papers but who cannot be legally expelled -- would take place while a new bill was being drafted for presentation to parliament.
Chevenement told parliament the new law would "set out a generous and realistic path" for French immigration policy while maintaining vigilance against clearly illegal immigration.
He accused the opposition of appealing to "feelings of fear" which were not based on the actual situation.

Rightist critics including ex-interior minister Jean-Louis Debre have predicted the new government initiative would lure more foreigners to France and bolster the extreme-right, which blames record 12.8 percent unemployment on illegal immigrants.
Opinion polls show that most voters favour the hardline approach taken by the previous government.
